title: Pan identifies a short-rate anchor as China’s credit aggregates lose information
summary: Speaking in Shanghai on 19 June 2024, PBoC Governor Pan Gongsheng described two developments that could look contradictory in market data. Monetary policy was supporting recovery, yet the growth of money and credit could slow as banks curtailed unproductive transactions and borrowers needed less new debt. His proposed solution was to give a short-term policy rate greater prominence and explain its transmission more clearly. The speech distinguished policies already in operation from institutional changes still under study. That distinction is central to reading either the funding curve or the bond market around the address. Pan supplied a direction for reform and a rationale for interpreting current credit data, without announcing a new policy rate or an immediate securities purchase (sections I and II, pp. 1–5).

Pan’s evidence for the current stance combined prices and quantities. Annual growth in aggregate financing to the real economy was 8.4% at end-May and M2 grew 7.0%. He compared those with first-quarter nominal GDP growth of 4.2%. These figures use different observation periods, so the comparison illustrates the relative pace of financing and output rather than the marginal growth generated by a yuan of credit. New loans issued in May carried a 3.67% rate. The PBoC had cut reserve requirements and policy rates and was supporting selected borrowers through targeted instruments. Outstanding structural instruments were roughly RMB 7 trillion, about 15% of the PBoC balance sheet. Measures on housing included lower minimum down payments, removal of mortgage rate floors and central-bank funding aimed at affordable housing. Each changes a different part of the financing decision: the required up-front payment, borrowing cost or availability of funding to a particular use (pp. 1–2).

The measured slowdown in financial quantities had several possible causes. The quarterly accounting method for financial-sector value added had shifted towards income, reducing the incentive for banks and local governments to inflate deposit and loan balances at reporting dates. The authorities had also acted against subsidised deposit gathering and the circulation of funds within the financial system. Meanwhile, property and local-government financing vehicles accounted for a large and declining share of almost RMB 250 trillion in loans. Growth in lending elsewhere first had to offset that contraction to register in total credit. Pan also pointed to the large starting stocks of M2 and social financing. A slower percentage growth rate can coexist with sizeable new financing off such a base. For a researcher, the question is which borrowers received funding and at what price, and whether that credit supported activity or merely replaced a maturing balance (pp. 2, 4–5).

Measurement itself was changing. Pan proposed reconsidering the coverage of M1 to reflect personal demand deposits and liquid products that could be used directly for payments. This was a proposal in the speech. Applying a future definition retrospectively without marking which data were available at the time would misrepresent the signals an investor could have seen that June. Pan also said specific numerical growth targets for money and financing had already given way to a qualitative alignment with nominal economic growth. He characterised credit demand as a more important constraint than before. If a firm refrains from investing, cheaper funding can be available even while new borrowing remains weak. The governor judged effective demand insufficient and saw a mild recovery in prices as desirable, subject to bank soundness and exchange-rate considerations (pp. 3–5).

For short rates, Pan nominated the seven-day reverse repo rate as already performing much of the work of a main policy rate. Less emphasis on other operational rates, an appropriately narrower corridor and loan prime rates that better represented actual prime borrowing costs could clarify transmission. He identified the standing lending facility rate as the ceiling and the rate paid on excess reserves as the floor of the existing wide corridor. Narrower money-market fluctuations were his evidence that a clearer signal could be feasible. For the lending channel, a small gap between the repo rate and interbank rates would establish control over marginal funding prices; it would not by itself demonstrate that loan rates, credit availability and spending responded across borrowers (p. 5).

The proposed secondary-market buying and selling of government bonds had a separate purpose. The PBoC had shifted towards open-market operations and medium-term lending as the earlier channel for base-money creation through foreign exchange diminished from 2014. Government-bond transactions could add a two-way liquidity instrument. Implementation and coordination with the Ministry of Finance, including issuance and market arrangements, were still being studied. Pan also drew attention to duration exposure at nonbanks holding longer bonds and expressed a preference for an upward-sloping yield curve. He gave neither a target yield nor a schedule of purchases. Therefore, a movement in long yields around the address could reflect investors’ reading of risk supervision, potential future operations or general policy accommodation. The text alone cannot separate these effects (pp. 5–6).

The external constraint also remained material. Pan noted the sizeable China–US interest-rate differential, increased use of currency hedges and a renminbi settlement share of about 30% for cross-border goods trade. The share measures the currency used for payment; it does not measure unhedged net exposures at individual firms. He expected a narrowing international policy-cycle divergence to ease pressure on domestic policy. His closing proposals favoured targeted credit instruments that could be withdrawn when their aims were met and clearer, more regular communication. In that light the most immediate market signal supplied by the speech was guidance on which prices and quantities to watch. An actual change in the size or maturity of the bank’s balance sheet would require subsequent transaction evidence (pp. 3, 6–7).

questions.question: Did the seven-day reverse repo rate become a more reliable signal for bank funding and loan pricing?
questions.detail: Measure spreads and volatility around the operational rate, then examine the relationship with other policy maturities, loan prime quotations and actual new-loan rates. Use announcement dates for subsequent operational changes separately from the June speech. Stronger interbank alignment with little change in banks’ actual prime lending prices would identify a break farther down the transmission chain.

questions.question: How much of weaker aggregate credit reflected productive reallocation, and how much reflected weaker demand?
questions.detail: Separate loan stocks and new flows for property, local financing vehicles and other borrowers. Compare these with lending rates, investment and survey measures of applications and approvals, allowing for changes in reporting incentives and monetary definitions. This would test whether more productive borrowers gained access while old loans ran off or whether lower borrowing costs coincided with weak demand across sectors.

questions.question: Would two-way bond operations move long-term yields mainly through liquidity or through duration exposure?
questions.detail: Track actual operation dates, purchases and sales, maturities, funding rates and parallel use of other central-bank tools. Examine whether reactions cluster at the short end or in the longer maturities held by nonbanks, and check bond issuance news. The distinction affects whether a fall in yields signals easier system-wide financing, scarcity of particular securities, or changing expectations about risk supervision.
